vignette: Elian sits across from me, hands folded over a worn leather portfolio that never seems to leave his side. He is forty-nine, an architect whose career has been built on load-bearing walls, precise calculations, and the quiet confidence of things that hold. Three years ago, on a rain-slicked site for a municipal renovation, the temporary scaffolding collapses during a sudden wind gust. Elian watches from the ground floor as two workers are dragged down in a tangle of steel and plaster. He runs toward them, boots slipping on wet concrete, and reaches out only to catch a wrist before it vanishes into the rubble. The paramedics later confirm the man survives, but the moment hardens in Elian's chest, cold and immovable. In the months that follow, Elian's mind reconstructs the collapse on repeat. He does not remember it so much as endure it. When he sits at his drafting table, the screech of tearing metal replaces the hum of his computer fans. He stops sleeping past three a.m., waking with his heart slamming against his ribs, convinced the ceiling of his bedroom is groaning under impossible weight. His wife, Clara, wakes frequently to find him sitting on the edge of the bed, fully dressed, staring at the door as if waiting for it to give way. He tries to describe the flashbacks to her, but the words keep coming out fractured: the angle of the fall, the way the dust cloud rolled like a storm front, the sudden quiet before the sirens. He begins measuring the width of doorways at home. He tells himself it is habit, but I watch his fingers tremble when he passes under low-hanging branches in the neighborhood park. Elian's practice shifts quietly. He stops taking site visits. When his firm offers him a lead role on a mixed-use high-rise, he declines without explanation, citing fatigue. His office, once a landscape of rolled blueprints and timber scale models, becomes a room he enters only by appointment. He avoids construction zones, rerouting his commute to take the river road instead, though it adds forty minutes to his day. At client meetings, he finds himself fixating on structural resilience rather than aesthetic vision. He asks developers about fire exits, steel grade histories, and maintenance logs with an intensity that unsettles the room. Inside, he wrestles with a quiet, relentless guilt. He replays the morning of the collapse and wonders if a different bracing calculation, a stricter inspection, a faster phone call could have kept the workers upright. The guilt does not scream; it seeps. It settles into his trapezius and thickens his voice when he speaks about next year. He says he feels like a ghost in his own profession, watching others draft futures while he traces the foundation lines of a building that no longer stands. Now, Elian's days are organized around anticipating what might trigger him. He keeps his apartment on the ground floor. He sleeps with the bedroom door open and a heavy wool blanket folded over the window. When Clara tries to plan a trip to visit her sister in Vancouver-a city whose skyline he once loved-he finds himself physically unable to pack a bag. His hand hovers over his passport, then drops to his side. He apologizes profusely, then retreats to his study to work on small residential commissions, drafting staircases that end abruptly on paper. I notice how his posture shifts when a siren passes outside: his breath catches, his gaze locks toward the street, and for a long moment, he is no longer in my office but back on that wet concrete, watching dust swallow the sky. He does not describe himself as broken. He describes himself as permanently braced. He sits in my chair now with the same rigid attention he once reserved for blueprints, as if every word must be measured, every silence accounted for, every threat anticipated.
